title: Integers and Rational Numbers
bigQuestion: How can a number be less than nothing, and how do we compare, locate and measure such numbers?

story.title: Minus Twenty on Lake Shore Drive
story.kicker: One January morning in Chicago, the thermometer dropped so far that the usual counting numbers ran out.
paragraphs: Marisol checked her phone before the walk to the bus. The screen said −20°F. Underneath, in smaller letters, it said 'feels like −41°F.' Her little brother Teo looked over her shoulder and asked the question every kid asks at some point: how can a temperature be less than zero? Zero sounds like nothing. How do you get colder than nothing?

Their dad, pulling on a second pair of gloves, said that zero on a Fahrenheit thermometer is not 'nothing.' It is just a mark someone chose. The mercury can sit at that mark, and it can sink below it. Every degree below zero gets a minus sign, so −20 means twenty degrees below the mark, and −41 means forty-one degrees below it. The colder it gets, the bigger the number after the minus sign, and the farther below zero you are.

Teo still wasn't satisfied. Which is colder, −20 or −41? Marisol drew a thermometer on the fogged window with her finger: a line, a zero in the middle, warm numbers going up, cold numbers going down. She marked −20 a little below zero and −41 much farther down. The lower mark is the colder one, she said, even though 41 is a bigger number than 20. That is the trick of negatives: farther from zero on the cold side means smaller.

On the bus, Marisol thought about all the other places numbers go below zero. The parking garage under her aunt's office building had levels labeled −1 and −2. Her older cousin's bank app once showed a balance of −$35 after a fee. The lowest point in Death Valley sits below sea level, and a diver's depth is written as a negative elevation. Numbers with a minus sign are everywhere once you start looking. The chapter you are starting is about those numbers: where they live, how to compare them, and how to measure the distance between them.
story.think: Which is colder, −20°F or −41°F? How could you convince someone who says 41 is bigger than 20, so −41 must be warmer?

lessons.title: Where Negative Numbers Live
lessons.mainIdea: A negative number tells how far below a chosen zero point something is, like a temperature, an elevation or a bank balance.
reading: A thermometer in Chicago in January might read −8°F. The minus sign means eight degrees below zero. Zero here is not 'nothing'; it is a mark on the scale. Numbers above the mark are *positive*, and numbers below it are *negative*. Every situation with a negative number has its own zero mark. For temperature, zero is a spot on the thermometer. For elevation, zero is sea level. For money, zero is having no money and owing none.

Try a few. A submarine 300 feet below the surface is at an elevation of −300 feet. A parking level two floors below the street is level −2. If you owe a friend $12 and have no cash, your money situation is −$12. A football team that loses 5 yards on a play has a gain of −5 yards. In each case, ask two questions: where is zero, and which direction counts as negative?

The whole numbers together with their negatives are called the *integers*: ..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... Zero is an integer, but it is neither positive nor negative. A common mistake is to read −300 feet as 'a big number' and think it means high. Remember that the minus sign points below zero; −300 feet is deep under the water, not far above it.

words.d: a number greater than zero, like 5 or 2.5
a number less than zero, written with a minus sign, like −5
the whole numbers and their opposites: ..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...

look.title: Temperatures in a Chicago Week
look.cite: example data, made up for this lesson
look.prompt: Which day was coldest? Which days were below zero? How much colder was Thursday than Monday?

check.q: A scuba diver is 45 feet below the surface of Lake Michigan. Which number shows her elevation?
check.why: Below sea level, or below the surface, is negative. Forty-five feet below is −45 feet.

check.q: Which of these is an integer?
check.why: Integers are whole numbers and their negatives. −7 is an integer; 1/2, −3.5 and 0.25 are not whole.

check.q: Your bank balance is −$20. What does that mean?
check.why: A negative balance means the account is below zero, so you owe the bank $20.

lessons.title: The Number Line in Both Directions
lessons.mainIdea: On a horizontal number line, positive numbers sit to the right of zero and negative numbers sit to the left, one unit apart.
reading: Draw a line. Put a tick in the middle and label it 0. To the right, mark 1, 2, 3, 4 at equal spaces. To the left, mark −1, −2, −3, −4 at the same spacing. This is a *number line* that runs both ways. Moving right always means the numbers get larger. Moving left always means they get smaller. So −4 is smaller than −1 because it is farther to the left.

To find −3 on the line, start at 0 and take three steps left. To find 2, start at 0 and take two steps right. The distance between −3 and 2 is 5 units: count the jumps −3 to −2, −2 to −1, −1 to 0, 0 to 1, 1 to 2. That is five jumps. Students sometimes count the tick marks instead of the jumps and get 6. Count the spaces, not the marks.

A vertical number line works the same way, with positive numbers above zero and negative numbers below. A thermometer is a vertical number line. An elevator panel with basement levels is a vertical number line. A horizontal one is handier for writing on paper. Either way, the rule is the same: numbers grow in one direction and shrink in the other, and the negatives are on the shrinking side of zero.

words.d: a line with 0 in the middle, positives on one side and negatives on the other, equally spaced

look.title: Walking the Line
look.text: Imagine a sidewalk with a chalk 0 in front of your feet. Chalk marks every meter run east (positive) and west (negative). You start at 0, walk 6 meters west, then turn and walk 9 meters east. Where do you end up? Then try this: start at −4 and walk 4 meters east.
look.prompt: Find each ending spot by counting the jumps, then write a rule for how walking east or west changes your number.

check.q: Which number sits farthest to the left on a number line?
check.why: Negative numbers are left of zero, and −9 is nine steps left, farther than −2.

check.q: How many units apart are −5 and 3 on the number line?
check.why: From −5 to 0 is 5 units, from 0 to 3 is 3 more; 5 + 3 = 8 units.

check.q: Start at −2 and move 6 units to the right. Where are you?
check.why: From −2, two steps right reach 0, and four more reach 4. So −2 + 6 = 4.

lessons.title: Opposites
lessons.mainIdea: Two numbers are opposites when they sit the same distance from zero on opposite sides, like 7 and −7.
reading: Take 7 on the number line. Its *opposite* is −7: the same distance from zero, but on the other side. The opposite of −3 is 3. The opposite of 0 is 0 itself, since 0 is neither left nor right of zero. We write 'the opposite of 7' as −7, and 'the opposite of −7' as −(−7), which equals 7. Two minus signs in a row bring you back to where you started.

Opposites show up when two things cancel. If you climb 40 feet and then descend 40 feet, your change in elevation is 40 + (−40) = 0. A team gains 8 yards and then loses 8 yards; net change, 0. That is the key property: a number plus its opposite is always 0. Chicago's Willis Tower is about 1,450 feet tall; going up to the top and back down is a change of +1,450 and −1,450, which sum to 0.

Do not confuse 'opposite' with 'reciprocal.' The opposite of 4 is −4 (flip the sign). The reciprocal of 4 is 1/4 (flip the fraction). Another slip: students see −(−5) and write −5, forgetting that the outer minus flips the sign of −5. Read it aloud: 'the opposite of negative five.' The opposite of a negative number is positive, so −(−5) = 5.

words.d: the number the same distance from zero on the other side; the opposite of 6 is −6

look.title: Elevator Trips
look.text: An elevator in a downtown building starts at the lobby, level 0. It goes up 12 floors to a dentist's office, then comes back down 12 floors. Later it goes down 3 levels to the garage, then up 3 levels. Write each trip as two numbers that are opposites and find where the elevator ends after each pair.
look.prompt: Why does every 'go and come back' trip end at zero? Write a rule using the word opposite.

check.q: What is the opposite of −12?
check.why: The opposite is the same distance from zero on the other side, so the opposite of −12 is 12.

check.q: What is −(−9)?
check.why: The opposite of −9 is 9. Two minus signs flip the sign twice, returning to positive.

check.q: A hiker climbs 250 feet and then descends 250 feet. What is the total change in elevation?
check.why: 250 and −250 are opposites; 250 + (−250) = 0.

lessons.title: Absolute Value
lessons.mainIdea: The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero, so it is never negative: |−6| = 6 and |6| = 6.
reading: How far is −6 from zero? Six steps. How far is 6 from zero? Also six steps. That distance is called the *absolute value*, and it is written with two bars: |−6| = 6 and |6| = 6. Distance is never negative, so absolute value is never negative. The absolute value of 0 is 0. A debt of −$35 has an absolute value of $35: that is the size of the debt, ignoring which direction it goes.

Absolute value answers 'how much' when direction does not matter. Two boats are at elevations −20 feet and 15 feet. Which one is farther from sea level? Compare |−20| = 20 and |15| = 15; the boat at −20 feet is farther, even though −20 is the smaller number. A temperature of −25°F is farther from zero than 18°F because |−25| = 25 is bigger than |18| = 18.

Two mistakes to watch. First, |−8| is 8, not −8; the bars strip away the sign. Second, students sometimes think the bigger absolute value means the bigger number. Not so: −25 has a bigger absolute value than 18, but −25 is smaller than 18. Absolute value measures size, not order. Keep 'how far from zero' and 'which is larger' as two separate questions.

words.d: a number's distance from zero, written with bars: |−4| = 4

look.title: Elevations Around North America
look.cite: rounded figures from U.S. Geological Survey and NOAA references
look.prompt: Which place is closest to sea level? Use absolute value to decide, then explain why the smallest number is not the answer.

check.q: What is |−14|?
check.why: Absolute value is distance from zero. −14 is 14 units from zero, so |−14| = 14.

check.q: Which number is farthest from zero?
check.why: Compare absolute values: 8, 3, 11, 10. The largest is |−11| = 11.

check.q: Two accounts have balances of −$60 and $45. Which statement is true?
choices: Both are the same distance from zero
check.why: |−60| = 60 and |45| = 45. Sixty is more, so −$60 is farther from zero, though it is the smaller balance.

lessons.title: Comparing Integers
lessons.mainIdea: Of two numbers on a number line, the one farther to the right is greater, so any positive beats any negative and −2 is greater than −9.
reading: Which is greater, −2 or −9? Picture the number line. −2 is two steps left of zero; −9 is nine steps left. Since −2 is farther to the right, −2 > −9. The symbol > means 'is greater than' and < means 'is less than.' The open side of the symbol faces the larger number. So we can also write −9 < −2. Students who compare only the digits would say 9 beats 2, but on the negative side the bigger digit means farther left, which means smaller.

Three quick rules follow from the number line. Any positive number is greater than any negative number: 1 > −100. Zero is greater than every negative number and less than every positive one. And for two negatives, the one with the smaller absolute value is greater: −3 > −7 because |−3| = 3 is less than |−7| = 7.

Try a real one. On a cold night Rockford reads −11°F and Chicago reads −6°F. Which city is warmer? −6 > −11, so Chicago is warmer by 5 degrees. In a game, one player has −40 points and another −15. Since −15 > −40, the player at −15 is ahead. Whenever you compare negatives, ask which one sits closer to zero; that one is greater.

words.d: farther right on the number line; written with >, as in 4 > −1
farther left on the number line; written with <, as in −8 < −2

look.title: Coldest to Warmest
look.text: Five cities report morning temperatures: Chicago −6°F, Minneapolis −14°F, St. Louis 9°F, Milwaukee −8°F, Springfield 0°F. Line them up from coldest to warmest. Then answer: which city is exactly at the zero mark, and how many degrees separate the coldest from the warmest?
look.prompt: Write the five temperatures in order using the < symbol between each pair.

check.q: Which comparison is true?
check.why: −3 is three left of zero, −7 is seven left. The one farther right, −3, is greater.

check.q: Which temperature is the warmest?
check.why: All are negative; the one closest to zero, −1, is farthest right and therefore warmest.

check.q: A student says −15 > −4 because 15 is more than 4. What is the mistake?
choices: The larger digit on the negative side means farther from zero, so smaller
check.why: On the negative side, a bigger absolute value means farther left. −15 < −4.

lessons.title: Ordering Rational Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: To order fractions, decimals and integers together, write them in one form, place them on the number line, and read from left to right.
reading: A *rational number* is any number that can be written as a fraction of two integers, like 3/4, −5/2, 0.6 or 7 (which is 7/1). To order a mix of them, put them in one form. Take −1.5, 3/4, −2, 0.25 and −1/2. Change the fractions to decimals: 3/4 = 0.75 and −1/2 = −0.5. Now the list is −1.5, 0.75, −2, 0.25, −0.5.

Place them on the line. Negatives go left: −2 is farthest left, then −1.5, then −0.5. Positives go right: 0.25, then 0.75. Read left to right: −2 < −1.5 < −0.5 < 0.25 < 0.75. Back in original form: −2 < −1.5 < −1/2 < 1/4 < 3/4. A common slip is to order the negatives as if they were positive, putting −0.5 before −2. Remember, on the left side of zero, the bigger absolute value is farther left.

Comparing two negative fractions works the same way. Which is greater, −2/3 or −3/4? As decimals, −2/3 ≈ −0.667 and −3/4 = −0.75. Since −0.667 is closer to zero, −2/3 > −3/4. Or use common denominators: −8/12 and −9/12; −8/12 is greater because it is only 8 twelfths below zero, not 9.

words.d: a number that can be written as a fraction of two integers, like −3/5, 0.8 or 4
arrange numbers from least to greatest, or greatest to least

look.title: Five Elevations
look.text: A geography project lists five spots by elevation in meters relative to sea level: a dock at −1.5, a beach at 0.5, a cellar at −3/4, a hilltop at 12.25 and a mine shaft at −8. Arrange the five spots from lowest to highest. Convert −3/4 to a decimal first.
look.prompt: Write the order from lowest to highest, then name the spot that is closest to sea level.

check.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest?
check.why: On the number line −3 is farthest left, then −1.5, then −0.5, then 2 on the right.

check.q: Which is greater, −3/5 or −4/5?
check.why: −3/5 = −0.6 and −4/5 = −0.8. The one closer to zero, −3/5, is greater.

check.q: Where does −1.25 belong among −2, −1, 0?
check.why: −1.25 is 1.25 below zero, which is past −1 but not as far as −2. So −2 < −1.25 < −1.

lessons.title: Fractions, Decimals and Repeating Digits
lessons.mainIdea: Every rational number has a decimal form that either ends or repeats, and you find it by dividing the top of the fraction by the bottom.
reading: To write 3/8 as a decimal, divide 3 by 8. Since 8 does not go into 3, write 3.000 and divide: 8 into 30 is 3 with remainder 6; 8 into 60 is 7 with remainder 4; 8 into 40 is 5 with no remainder. So 3/8 = 0.375. The decimal *terminates*, meaning it stops. Fractions whose bottoms divide evenly into a power of ten, like 8, 4, 5 and 20, always terminate.

Now try 2/3. Divide 2 by 3: 3 into 20 is 6, remainder 2; 3 into 20 is 6 again, remainder 2 again. The same remainder keeps coming back, so the same digit repeats forever: 2/3 = 0.6666... We write a *repeating decimal* with a bar over the repeating part, or in plain text as 0.666... For 5/11 the remainders cycle 5, 6, 5, 6, giving 0.454545... The block '45' repeats.

Going the other way, a decimal that ends is easy to turn into a fraction: 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20. A negative rational number works the same: −0.375 = −3/8. The important fact is that every fraction of integers gives a decimal that either stops or falls into a repeating pattern, because there are only so many possible remainders. A decimal that never stops and never repeats, like the digits of π, is not rational; you will meet those in Chapter 28.

words.d: to stop; a terminating decimal like 0.375 has a last digit
a decimal whose digits fall into a block that repeats forever, like 0.666...

look.title: Fractions With Denominator 9
look.cite: computed by dividing top by bottom
look.prompt: What pattern do the decimals follow? Predict 7/9 and 8/9 before you divide, then check by division.

check.q: What is 5/8 as a decimal?
check.why: Divide 5 by 8: 8 into 50 is 6 (r 2), 8 into 20 is 2 (r 4), 8 into 40 is 5. So 5/8 = 0.625.

check.q: Which fraction gives a repeating decimal?
check.why: 1/3 = 0.333... repeats. The others end: 0.75, 0.35 and 1.125.

check.q: Which fraction equals −0.6?

lessons.title: Four Quadrants
lessons.mainIdea: Two number lines crossing at zero make a coordinate plane, and their signs split it into four quadrants.
reading: Lay a horizontal number line on the page. Now stand a vertical number line on it so the two zeros touch. The horizontal line is the *x-axis*, the vertical line is the *y-axis*, and the point where they cross is the *origin*. Together they form the *coordinate plane*. The axes cut the plane into four regions called quadrants, numbered with Roman numerals I, II, III, IV, starting at the upper right and going counterclockwise.

Every point on the plane gets a pair of numbers (x, y). The first number tells how far left or right of the origin; the second tells how far up or down. The signs tell you the quadrant. Quadrant I: both positive, like (3, 2). Quadrant II: x negative, y positive, like (−3, 2). Quadrant III: both negative, like (−3, −2). Quadrant IV: x positive, y negative, like (3, −2).

Chicago's street grid works like this. State Street and Madison Street cross at the city's origin. Addresses are north, south, east or west of that corner. An address at 800 North and 1200 West is like the point (−1200, 800): west is negative x, north is positive y. That would be Quadrant II. A point on an axis, like (0, 4) or (−5, 0), is not in any quadrant; it sits on the border.

words.d: the horizontal number line in a coordinate plane
the vertical number line in a coordinate plane
the point (0, 0) where the two axes cross
a flat surface with an x-axis and a y-axis, where every point has an (x, y) address

look.title: Sorting Points by Sign
look.text: Here are six points: (4, 7), (−2, 5), (−6, −1), (3, −8), (0, −5), (−9, 0). For each one, decide which quadrant it belongs to, or whether it sits on an axis. Do it by signs alone, without drawing. Then draw a quick sketch and check.
look.prompt: Which points are not in any quadrant, and why? Write a rule for spotting Quadrant III from the signs.

check.q: In which quadrant is the point (−5, −3)?
check.why: Both coordinates are negative: left of the origin and below it. That is Quadrant III.

check.q: Which point lies in Quadrant IV?
check.why: Quadrant IV has positive x and negative y, so (6, −2) is right of the origin and below it.

check.q: Where is the point (0, −7)?
check.why: x = 0 means no left or right movement; the point sits on the vertical y-axis, 7 units below the origin.

lessons.title: Plotting Points
lessons.mainIdea: To plot (x, y), start at the origin, move x units left or right, then y units up or down, and mark the spot.
reading: Plot (−4, 3). Start at the origin. The x-coordinate is −4, so move 4 units left along the x-axis. The y-coordinate is 3, so from there move 3 units up. Mark the point. Now plot (2, −5): from the origin move 2 right, then 5 down. The order matters. The *ordered pair* always lists x first, then y. Swapping them puts the point in a different spot: (3, 1) and (1, 3) are not the same.

Reading a point works in reverse. Look straight up or down from the point to the x-axis and read the number; that is x. Look left or right to the y-axis; that is y. A point directly below −6 on the x-axis and level with 2 on the y-axis is (−6, 2). A common error is reading a point on the left side as positive because the student forgets which way is negative. Left is negative, down is negative.

Coordinates make shapes. Plot A(−3, 1), B(3, 1), C(3, −2) and D(−3, −2) and connect them in order. You get a rectangle. Its width runs from x = −3 to x = 3, which is 6 units. Its height runs from y = −2 to y = 1, which is 3 units. Its area is 6 × 3 = 18 square units. Maps, video games and graphs all locate things this same way.

words.d: two numbers (x, y) that name a point; x comes first
one of the two numbers in an ordered pair

look.title: Draw the Path
look.text: A robot in a warehouse starts at the origin. It visits (5, 0), then (5, −4), then (−2, −4), then (−2, 3), then returns to (0, 0). Sketch the path on grid paper. Each grid unit is 1 meter. The robot only moves along grid lines, horizontally or vertically.
look.prompt: How many meters does the robot travel in total? Count each leg by subtracting coordinates, then add the legs.

check.q: To plot (−2, 6), which moves do you make from the origin?
check.why: x = −2 means 2 units left; y = 6 means 6 units up.

check.q: A point sits 4 units right of the y-axis and 1 unit below the x-axis. What are its coordinates?
check.why: Right of the y-axis means x = 4; below the x-axis means y = −1. The pair is (4, −1).

check.q: The points (−1, 2), (5, 2), (5, −1), (−1, −1) form a rectangle. What is its area?
check.why: Width from x = −1 to x = 5 is 6 units; height from y = −1 to y = 2 is 3 units; area 6 × 3 = 18.

lessons.title: Distances on the Plane
lessons.mainIdea: Two points on the same horizontal or vertical line are as far apart as the difference of their unequal coordinates, found with absolute values.
reading: How far is (−3, 4) from (5, 4)? Both points have y = 4, so they sit on the same horizontal line. Only the x-coordinates differ. From −3 to 0 is 3 units, from 0 to 5 is 5 more, so the distance is 8. Using absolute value: |−3| + |5| = 3 + 5 = 8. When the two x-values have opposite signs, add their absolute values, because the path crosses the y-axis.

Now (2, −6) and (2, −1). Same x, so the line is vertical. Both y-values are negative, on the same side of zero. Distance is the difference of their absolute values: |−6| − |−1| = 6 − 1 = 5. Check by counting on the y-axis from −6 up to −1: five jumps. The general rule: same signs, subtract the absolute values; opposite signs, add them. Or, in one step, take the absolute value of the difference: |−6 − (−1)| = |−5| = 5.

A common mistake is subtracting the numbers without care and getting a negative distance. Distance is never negative, so if your answer has a minus sign, take its absolute value. Another slip is trying to find the distance between points that share neither coordinate this way; for those you need a right triangle and the Pythagorean theorem, which comes later. In this chapter, stick to points that line up horizontally or vertically.

words.d: how far apart two points are, always zero or positive

look.title: Blocks Across the Loop
look.text: Picture Chicago's downtown grid as a coordinate plane with the origin at State and Madison and each unit as one block. A café sits at (−3, 2) and a library at (4, 2). A bus stop is at (4, −5). Find the distance from the café to the library, then from the library to the bus stop.
look.prompt: Which is longer, the café-to-library walk or the library-to-bus-stop walk? Show the absolute value work for each.

check.q: What is the distance between (−7, 1) and (2, 1)?
check.why: Same y, opposite-sign x-values: |−7| + |2| = 7 + 2 = 9.

check.q: What is the distance between (3, −8) and (3, −2)?
check.why: Same x, both y-values negative: |−8| − |−2| = 8 − 2 = 6. Or |−8 − (−2)| = |−6| = 6.

check.q: Two points are (−4, 5) and (−4, −5). Which method gives the distance?
choices: Add the absolute values of the y-coordinates: 5 + 5 = 10
check.why: Same x, y-values on opposite sides of zero. Add the absolute values: |5| + |−5| = 10.

lessons.title: Reflections Across the Axes
lessons.mainIdea: Changing the sign of one coordinate reflects a point across an axis: (x, y) to (−x, y) flips it over the y-axis, and (x, y) to (x, −y) flips it over the x-axis.
reading: Take the point (3, 5). Change the sign of x to get (−3, 5). On the plane, the new point is the mirror image of the old one across the y-axis: same height, same distance from the axis, opposite side. Now change the sign of y instead: (3, −5). That is the reflection across the x-axis, straight below the original. Change both signs, (−3, −5), and the point lands in the opposite quadrant, diagonally across the origin.

This is why opposites matter on the plane. (3, 5) and (−3, 5) are the same distance from the y-axis, 3 units each, so the distance between them is 6. (3, 5) and (3, −5) are each 5 units from the x-axis, so they are 10 apart. Symmetric designs, like a butterfly drawing or a logo, are often built by plotting one half and reflecting every point.

Try it. A triangle has corners at (1, 2), (4, 2) and (4, 6). Reflect it across the x-axis by changing every y to its opposite: (1, −2), (4, −2), (4, −6). Reflect the original across the y-axis instead: (−1, 2), (−4, 2), (−4, 6). A common mistake is changing the wrong coordinate. Remember that reflecting across the y-axis moves you left or right, so x changes; reflecting across the x-axis moves you up or down, so y changes.

words.d: a flip of a point or shape across a line, producing a mirror image

look.title: Mirror the Kite
look.text: Half of a kite is drawn in Quadrant I with corners at (0, 6), (3, 3) and (0, −2). The kite's line of symmetry is the y-axis. Find the missing corner by reflecting (3, 3) across the y-axis. Then list all four corners of the full kite and find its width from side to side.
look.prompt: Which coordinate changed when you reflected, and why did the two points on the y-axis stay the same?

check.q: What is the reflection of (−6, 2) across the x-axis?
check.why: Reflecting across the x-axis changes the sign of y only: (−6, 2) becomes (−6, −2).

check.q: What is the reflection of (−6, 2) across the y-axis?
check.why: Reflecting across the y-axis changes the sign of x only: (−6, 2) becomes (6, 2).

check.q: How far apart are (7, −3) and its reflection across the y-axis?
check.why: The reflection is (−7, −3). Same y, opposite-sign x: |7| + |−7| = 14.

review.why: −18 is farthest left on the number line, 18 units below zero.
Absolute value is distance from zero; −25 is 25 units away.

review.q: What is the opposite of the opposite of −4?
review.why: The opposite of −4 is 4; the opposite of 4 is −4. Two flips return to −4.
7 ÷ 8: 8 into 70 is 8 (r 6), 8 into 60 is 7 (r 4), 8 into 40 is 5. So 0.875.

review.q: Which list is ordered from least to greatest?
review.why: −1/2 = −0.5. Left to right: −2, then −0.75, then −0.5, then 1.
x positive, y negative means right of the origin and below it: Quadrant IV.

review.q: What is the distance between (−5, −2) and (−5, 6)?
review.why: Same x; y-values on opposite sides of zero: |−2| + |6| = 2 + 6 = 8.

review.q: A thermometer reads −9°F at dawn. Which later reading is warmer?
review.why: The warmer temperature is closer to zero (farther right). −6 > −9; the others are all lower.
